nike.name: Nike
nike.fact: Nike describes its mission around inspiration and innovation for athletes.
nike.hypothesis: Running-focused messaging may resonate with people who identify with athletic progress. This is a hypothesis, not an observed audience segment.
nike.test: Compare a personal-progress message with a product-feature message in a randomized creative experiment.
nike.metric: Predefine conversion rate as the primary metric, with cost per conversion as a guardrail. Use a power calculation before launch.
nike.gap: These company materials do not measure campaign reach, audience size, conversion lift or ROAS.

starbucks.name: Starbucks
starbucks.fact: Starbucks presents its business around coffee and the coffeehouse experience.
starbucks.hypothesis: A coffeehouse-experience message may resonate differently from a convenience message. The current evidence does not establish which audience prefers either.
starbucks.test: Compare an experience-led message with a convenience-led message under the same eligibility and allocation rules.
starbucks.metric: Choose one conversion event before running the test; monitor cost and uncertainty rather than selecting a winner from clicks alone.
starbucks.gap: Company descriptions do not establish current customer demographics, campaign results or incremental sales.

tesla.name: Tesla
tesla.fact: Tesla presents products spanning electric vehicles and energy systems.
tesla.hypothesis: Vehicle and home-energy buyers may need different messages. This segmentation is an inferred starting point, not measured customer data.
tesla.test: Within one product campaign, compare a product-utility message with an ownership-experience message. Avoid comparing unrelated product audiences as if randomized.
tesla.metric: Predefine qualified lead conversion rate and acquisition cost; review whether leads remain qualified downstream.
tesla.gap: This evidence does not provide geographic eligibility, current product availability, audience overlap or campaign performance.
